claims.claim: The insect immune system shares many fundamental traits with higher vertebrates.
claims.source: Critically, despite the small size and modest cellular complexity, the insect immune system shares many fundamental traits with the higher vertebrates, including the humoral and innate arms and the dialogue between the two (Hultmark, 1993; Adams et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The insect immune system includes humoral and innate arms.
claims.source: Critically, despite the small size and modest cellular complexity, the insect immune system shares many fundamental traits with the higher vertebrates, including the humoral and innate arms and the dialogue between the two (Hultmark, 1993; Adams et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Several factors that contribute to the proper functioning of the insect immune system are highly conserved and perform analogous functions across evolution.
claims.source: Furthermore, several factors that contribute to the proper functioning of the insect immune system are highly conserved and perform analogous functions across evolution (Hoffmann and Reichhart, 2002; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Almost all protein components of the insect immune system are highly pleiotropic and involve diverse activities during developmental progression.
claims.source: Interestingly, almost all the protein components of the insect immune system are highly pleiotropic and involve diverse activities during developmental progression.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Toll class proteins are essential for mounting robust immune response against microorganismal invasion.
claims.source: For example, the Toll class of proteins belonging to a larger family of pattern recognition receptors are essential while mounting robust immune response against the microorganismal invasion (Brennan and Anderson, 2004; Wang and Ligoxygakis, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Toll proteins are deployed during embryonic patterning and morphogenesis.
claims.source: The same proteins are also deployed earlier during embryonic patterning and morphogenesis (Govind, 1999; Hoffmann and Reichhart, 2002; Valanne et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dorsal is involved in both Dorso-ventral patterning and humoral response in flies.
claims.source: The involvement of early embryonic morphogen, Dorsal, during humoral response in flies is a canonical example of the context-specific and diverse functions of immune system components (Govind, 1999; Roth, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Maternal loss of function of genes involved in Toll/Dorsal signaling affect Dorso-ventral patterning.
claims.source: Maternal loss of function of genes involved in Toll/Dorsal signaling affect Dorso-ventral patterning (Belvin and Anderson, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: A nuclear-cytoplasmic gradient of Dorsal, set up by asymmetric Toll signalling, establishes cell fate across the Dorsal-ventral axis in the syncytial embryo.
claims.source: A nuclear-cytoplasmic gradient of Dorsal, set up by asymmetric Toll signalling establishes cell fate across the Dorsal-ventral axis in the syncytial embryo (Nüsslein-Volhard, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Pathogenic invasion of insects induces both the humoral and cellular immune response.
claims.source: Pathogenic invasion of insects induces both the humoral and cellular immune response (Belvin and Anderson, 1996; Williams, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The humoral response consists of the production of antimicrobial peptides by the fat bodies.
claims.source: The humoral response consists of the production of antimicrobial peptides by the fat bodies, which serve as a first line of defence (Belvin and Anderson, 1996; Imler and Hoffmann, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dorsal and Dif are Rel family member proteins homologous to mammalian NF-kappa B.
claims.source: Two Rel family member proteins, Dorsal and Dif, homologous to the mammalian NF-kappa B, induce the expression of defense peptides (Belvin and Anderson, 1996; Govind, 1999; Buchon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dorsal and Dif induce the expression of defense peptides.
claims.source: Two Rel family member proteins, Dorsal and Dif, homologous to the mammalian NF-kappa B, induce the expression of defense peptides (Belvin and Anderson, 1996; Govind, 1999; Buchon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: NF-kappa B is essential for differentiating lymphocytes.
claims.source: NF-kappa B is essential for differentiating lymphocytes, which engineer the acute-phase response.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claims.claim: Casp is an intracellular negative regulator discovered in a genetic screen to identify suppressors of antibacterial immunity.
claims.source: Casp is an intracellular negative regulator discovered in a genetic screen to identify suppressors of antibacterial immunity (Kim et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Flies mutant for casp were identified due to their high rates of melanization.
claims.source: Flies mutant for casp were identified due to their high rates of melanization, an innate immune response that leads to encapsulation of pathogens in the gut and fat body.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: casp mutants were resistant to Gram-negative bacterial infections due to elevated expression of the antimicrobial peptide diptericin.
claims.source: Interestingly, casp mutants isolated in this study were resistant to Gram-negative bacterial infections due to elevated expression of the antimicrobial peptide (AMP) diptericin; consequently, infected flies survived longer than their wild-type counterparts.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: casp overexpression inhibited nuclear localization of Rel in response to infection in the fat body.
claims.source: Strikingly, casp overexpression inhibited nuclear localization of Rel in response to infection in the fat body.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Excess levels of Casp result in the cytoplasmic retention of Rel in its uncleaved, inactive form.
claims.source: Excess levels of Casp result in the cytoplasmic retention of Rel in its uncleaved, inactive form, presumably due to inhibition of the protease, Dredd (Kim et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Casp shows a high degree of similarity to the mammalian Fas-associated factor 1 (FAF1) protein.
claims.source: Intriguingly, sequence analysis of Casp indicated a high degree of similarity to the mammalian Fas-associated factor 1 (FAF1) protein (Kim et al., 2006; Tendulkar et al., 2022; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents sequence comparison data and refers to Figure 1A showing domain conservation.

claims.claim: FAF1 is evolutionarily conserved.
claims.source: FAF1 is evolutionarily conserved and was initially discovered as an interactor of Fas, a pro-apoptotic member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor family (Chu et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: FAF1 was initially discovered as an interactor of Fas.
claims.source: FAF1 is evolutionarily conserved and was initially discovered as an interactor of Fas, a pro-apoptotic member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor family (Chu et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Fas is a pro-apoptotic member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor family.
claims.source: FAF1 is evolutionarily conserved and was initially discovered as an interactor of Fas, a pro-apoptotic member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor family (Chu et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge.

claims.claim: FAF1 interacts with components of the death-inducing signaling complex (DISC) such as FADD and Caspase-8 proteins.
claims.source: FAF1 also interacts with the components of the death-inducing signaling complex (DISC) such as the Fas-associated death domain (FADD) and Caspase-8 proteins (Ryu et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The interactions between FAF1 and DISC components are mediated by the death effector domains (DED) in FADD and Caspase-8 and the DED-interacting domain (DEDID) in FAF1.
claims.source: These interactions are mediated by the death effector domains (DED) in FADD and Caspase-8 and the DED-interacting domain (DEDID) in FAF1 (Ryu et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: FAF1 is crucial in promoting cell death via transduction of the apoptotic signal.
claims.source: Both 'loss' and 'gain' of function experiments indicated that FAF1 is crucial in promoting cell death via transduction of the apoptotic signal (Ryu and Kim, 2001; De Zio et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: FAF1 is a negative regulator of NFκB signalling.
claims.source: FAF1, like its Drosophila ortholog, is a negative regulator of NFκB signalling (Min-Young et al., 2004; Park et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: FAF1 harbors a Ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain, a UAS domain and a Ubiquitin-like regulatory X (UBX) domain.
claims.source: Consistently, FAF1 harbors a Ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain, a UAS domain and a Ubiquitin-like regulatory X (UBX) domain (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the domain structure and refers to Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The N-terminal UBA domain of FAF1 recruits polyubiquitinated proteins, leading to their accumulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, the N-terminal UBA domain recruits polyubiquitinated proteins, leading to their accumulation (Song et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The C-terminal UBX domain of FAF1 interacts with the molecular chaperone VCP/p97 bound to the Npl4-Ufd1 heterodimeric complex.
claims.source: The C-terminal UBX domain, on the other hand, interacts with the molecular chaperone, valosin-containing protein (VCP/p97) bound to the Npl4-Ufd1 heterodimeric complex (Schuberth and Buchberger, 2008; Kloppsteck et al., 2012; Ewens et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: FAF1 complexed with VCP-Npl4-Ufd1 and polyubiquitinated proteins assists endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD).
claims.source: FAF1 complexed with VCP-Npl4-Ufd1 and polyubiquitinated proteins is known to assist endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD; Lee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The UAS domain of FAF1 is involved in interaction with long-chain fatty acids, which is thought to promote the polymerization of FAF1.
claims.source: The UAS domain, a domain of unknown function, is involved in interaction with long-chain fatty acids, which is thought to promote the polymerization of FAF1 (Kim et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: casp is highly expressed in the 0–3 hr old embryo.
claims.source: While Casp has a well-established role in the immune response, modENCODE RNAseq and proteomics data suggest that casp is also highly expressed in the 0–3 hr old embryo (Brown et al., 2014; Casas-Vila et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on published database data.

claims.claim: Maternally deposited casp is ubiquitously expressed in the Drosophila embryo.
claims.source: Consistently, a snapshot of casp staining in a high-throughput RNA in situ experiment indicates ubiquitous expression of maternally deposited casp in the Drosophila embryo (Weiszmann et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is based on published in situ hybridization data.

claims.claim: Approximately 70% of embryos laid by homozygous casplof females failed to hatch into larvae.
claims.source: ~70% embryos laid by the homozygous casplof females failed to hatch into larvae (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data quantifying embryonic lethality.

claims.claim: The extent of viability in casplof embryos was independent of the paternal genotype.
claims.source: Moreover, the number of embryos that failed to hatch did not change substantially when casplof virgin females were mated either with w1118 males or casplof males.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from crosses with different paternal genotypes.

claims.claim: casp is a maternal effect gene.
claims.source: That the extent of viability was independent of the paternal genotype established that casp is a maternal effect gene and its activity is required for viability (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic crosses showing maternal-specific effects.

claims.claim: casplof/Df mothers displayed significant embryonic lethality (40%).
claims.source: To rule out the possibility that the lethality was induced by non-specific background mutations, we procured multiple deficiency (Df) lines spanning the 52D locus and confirmed that casplof/Df mothers also displayed significant embryonic lethality (40%; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data using deficiency lines to confirm the phenotype.

claims.claim: casplof males are semi-fertile.
claims.source: Lastly, as in the case of casplof females, casplof males are also semi-fertile which was assessed by mating the mutant males with w1118 virgin females (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data on male fertility.

claims.claim: casp mRNA is deposited maternally and is highly expressed in the 0–2 hr embryo.
claims.source: Consistent with the maternal effect lethality, modENCODE (Muers, 2011; Chen et al., 2014) data suggests that casp mRNA is deposited maternally, being highly expressed in the 0–2 hr embryo, with a drop in expression 2–4 hr post fertilization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Brown et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on published database data.

claims.claim: casp mRNA expression drops 2–4 hr post fertilization.
claims.source: Consistent with the maternal effect lethality, modENCODE (Muers, 2011; Chen et al., 2014) data suggests that casp mRNA is deposited maternally, being highly expressed in the 0–2 hr embryo, with a drop in expression 2–4 hr post fertilization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Brown et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on published database data.

claims.claim: casp mRNA is ubiquitously expressed in stage 1–3 embryos.
claims.source: Publicly available in-situ databases such as FlyAtlas, Fly-FISH, and BDGP (Weiszmann et al., 2009; Tomancak et al., 2002; Lécuyer et al., 2007) also confirmed maternal deposition of casp mRNA, with ubiquitous expression seen in stage 1–3 embryos.
claims.evidence: This is based on published in situ hybridization databases.

claims.claim: casp expression in the pole cells persists while maternally deposited somatic transcripts are selectively degraded from stage 4 onwards.
claims.source: Fly-FISH data (Lécuyer et al., 2007; Wilk et al., 2016) further suggests that expression in the pole cells persists while maternally deposited somatic transcripts are selectively degraded from stage 4 onwards.
claims.evidence: This is based on published in situ hybridization data.

claims.claim: Casp protein is predominantly cytoplasmic in 0- to 3-hr-old embryos.
claims.source: We immunostained 0- to 3-hr-old embryos derived from w1118 mothers with the anti-Casp antibody (Tendulkar et al., 2022) and found that Casp protein was predominantly cytoplasmic, and as in the case of RNA, exhibited a relatively ubiquitous distribution in the somatic compartment (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing subcellular localization.

claims.claim: Casp protein is enriched in posteriorly localized PGCs compared to the surrounding soma.
claims.source: Again, consistent with the in situ hybridization pattern, Casp-specific antibody staining appeared to be enriched in the posteriorly localized PGCs compared to the surrounding soma (Figure 1D, arrow).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing enrichment in PGCs.

claims.claim: Casp protein is nearly absent in embryos of casplof/casplof and casplof/Df genotypes.
claims.source: To establish the specificity of the anti-Casp antibodies in the embryonic context, we stained the embryos laid by both the casplof/ casplof and casplof/Df mothers. As expected, Casp protein was nearly absent in embryos of both these genotypes suggesting that Casp protein is significantly reduced in the 0- to 3-hr-old casplof mutant embryos.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing loss of signal in mutants.

claims.claim: Trace amounts of Casp protein (estimated 5–10% of w1118) are present in embryos laid by casplof/casplof and casplof/Df mothers.
claims.source: Analysis of the embryonic lysates using western blotting, suggested that trace amounts of Casp protein (estimated 5–10% of w1118), were present in embryos laid by casplof/casplof and casplof/Df mothers, supporting the conclusion that casplof is a strong hypomorphic allele and not a null (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data quantifying protein levels.

claims.claim: casplof is a strong hypomorphic allele and not a null.
claims.source: Analysis of the embryonic lysates using western blotting, suggested that trace amounts of Casp protein (estimated 5–10% of w1118), were present in embryos laid by casplof/casplof and casplof/Df mothers, supporting the conclusion that casplof is a strong hypomorphic allele and not a null (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from western blot data showing residual protein.

claims.claim: Mature egg chambers of wild-type animals have Casp expression in somatically derived follicle cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, mature egg chambers of wild-type animals had Casp expression in somatically derived follicle cells, but Casp protein could not be readily detected in the egg itself (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data of egg chambers.

claims.claim: Only trace amounts of Casp protein may be maternally deposited in the egg.
claims.source: This observation suggested that, unlike the RNA, only trace amounts of Casp protein may be maternally deposited.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining data of egg chambers.

claims.claim: The Casp protein detected in young embryos is likely generated post-fertilization by translation of maternally deposited casp mRNA.
claims.source: Thus, the protein detected in the young embryos is likely generated post-fertilization, by the translation of maternally deposited casp mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mRNA but not protein is maternally deposited.

claims.claim: Approximately 60% of larvae from casplof/Df mothers displayed cuticular patterns comparable to wild type larvae.
claims.source: While ~60% of larvae displayed cuticular patterns comparable to wild type larvae, development in the remaining 40% embryos appeared to have stalled before they could deposit cuticle.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents cuticle preparation data.

claims.claim: Development in 40% of embryos from casplof/Df mothers stalled before they could deposit cuticle.
claims.source: While ~60% of larvae displayed cuticular patterns comparable to wild type larvae, development in the remaining 40% embryos appeared to have stalled before they could deposit cuticle.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents cuticle preparation data.

claims.claim: 40% of casplof embryos did not proceed to gastrulation and showed developmental arrest before germ band extension (around stage 6).
claims.source: These data (Movies, Figure 1—videos 1–3) confirmed that 40% of embryos did not proceed to gastrulation and showed developmental arrest before germ band extension (around stage 6; Figure 1—figure supplement 2 B4, C4).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: casplof embryos displayed irregular, uncoordinated morphogenetic movements with blebbing of the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Such embryos displayed irregular, uncoordinated morphogenetic movements with blebbing of the plasma membrane possibly inhibiting both cephalic furrow formation, and germband elongation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 B2, B3, C2, C3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging data showing morphogenetic defects.

claims.claim: casplof embryos display significant structural abnormalities including an irregular actin network that lacks stereotypical organization.
claims.source: casplof embryos displayed significant structural abnormalities that are reflected in an irregular actin network that lacks stereotypical organization, which is partially interrupted in several places (Figure 2 B1 compared to Figure 2 A1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing cytoskeletal defects.

claims.claim: In casplof embryos, regular nuclear spacing is disrupted, and nuclei are unevenly distributed across the embryo.
claims.source: Similarly, unlike the age-matched control embryos, regular nuclear spacing is disrupted, and nuclei are unevenly distributed across the embryo with occasional instances of nuclear fusion and possibly mitotic asynchrony (Figure 2B vs Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing nuclear defects.

claims.claim: casplof embryos show occasional instances of nuclear fusion and possibly mitotic asynchrony.
claims.source: Similarly, unlike the age-matched control embryos, regular nuclear spacing is disrupted, and nuclei are unevenly distributed across the embryo with occasional instances of nuclear fusion and possibly mitotic asynchrony (Figure 2B vs Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing nuclear defects.

claims.claim: In casplof embryos, several characteristic aspects of centrosome behavior during mitotic divisions are altered.
claims.source: In the embryos maternally compromised for casp, several characteristic aspects of centrosome behavior during mitotic divisions are altered (compare Figure 2 B3 to Figure 2 A3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing centrosome defects.

claims.claim: In casplof embryos, centrosomes appeared to divide even without a nucleus (or DNA), and many 'orphan' centrosomes devoid of nuclear DNA were observed.
claims.source: At times, centrosomes appeared to divide even without a nucleus (or DNA), and many 'orphan' centrosomes devoid of nuclear DNA were observed (Figure 2 B3, inset).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing centrosome defects.

claims.claim: In casplof embryos, centrosomes were duplicated but remained in proximity indicating failed or incomplete migration.
claims.source: By contrast, in some instances, centrosomes were duplicated but remained in proximity indicating failed or incomplete migration (see arrows in Figure 2 B3, inset).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing centrosome defects.

claims.claim: The behavior of centrosomes in casplof embryos, especially their ability to separate and migrate to the opposite poles correctly, deteriorated progressively as nuclear division cycles advanced.
claims.source: Quantitation of the centrosomal abnormalities in casplof embryos (Figure 2C and D) further revealed that the behavior of the centrosomes, especially their ability to separate and migrate to the opposite poles correctly deteriorated progressively (compare Figure 2D to Figure 2C), as nuclear division cycles advanced.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data showing progressive worsening of centrosome defects.

claims.claim: Maternal overexpression of casp substantially rescues centrosomal and cytoskeletal abnormalities seen in casplof.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2E, maternal overexpression of casp substantially rescues centrosomal and cytoskeletal abnormalities seen in casplof (compare panels E1-E3 to A1-A3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing rescue of defects.

claims.claim: casplof/Df; nos Gal4/UASp-caspwt showed a rescue of lethality of 20–25% as compared to 40–45% for casplof/Df.
claims.source: The casplof/Df; nos Gal4/UASp-caspwt showed a rescue of lethality of 20–25% as compared to 40–45% for casplof/Df.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents viability data showing partial rescue.

claims.claim: Casp plays an essential role in early embryonic development in Drosophila.
claims.source: Taken together, these data showed that Casp plays an essential role in early embryonic development in Drosophila, and loss of casp results in conspicuous nuclear and cytoskeletal defects that correlate with incomplete gastrulation movements and developmental arrest, for ~45% of embryos.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: Loss of casp results in conspicuous nuclear and cytoskeletal defects that correlate with incomplete gastrulation movements and developmental arrest for ~45% of embryos.
claims.source: Taken together, these data showed that Casp plays an essential role in early embryonic development in Drosophila, and loss of casp results in conspicuous nuclear and cytoskeletal defects that correlate with incomplete gastrulation movements and developmental arrest, for ~45% of embryos.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents multiple types of data supporting this conclusion.

claims.claim: The defects in casplof embryos do not appear to be region-specific or localized within an embryo.
claims.source: Moreover, such defects do not appear to be region-specific or localized within an embryo arguing in support of ubiquitous function across the embryo for Casp protein.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of defects throughout the embryo.

claims.claim: Casp protein has ubiquitous function across the embryo.
claims.source: Moreover, such defects do not appear to be region-specific or localized within an embryo arguing in support of ubiquitous function across the embryo for Casp protein.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the widespread nature of defects.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, PGCs are formed in the posterior end of the embryo.
claims.source: In Drosophila, the PGCs are formed in the posterior end of the embryo.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in Drosophila developmental biology.

claims.claim: During early embryonic development, a few nuclei and centrosomes invade posteriorly localized and anchored pole plasm ahead of the rest of the somatic nuclei.
claims.source: As the early embryonic syncytial nuclear division cycles progress, a few nuclei and centrosomes associated with them invade posteriorly localized and anchored pole plasm ahead of the rest of the somatic nuclei (Raff and Glover, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The precocious entry of centrosomes results in the release and microtubule-dependent transport of pole plasm, which is sequestered in newly cellularized PGCs.
claims.source: The precocious entry of the centrosomes results in the release and microtubule-dependent transport of pole plasm, which is sequestered in newly cellularized PGCs (Raff and Glover, 1989; Lerit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Centrosome behavior and dynamics are crucial for proper cellularization and mitotic cell divisions of early germ cells.
claims.source: Moreover, centrosome behavior and dynamics are crucial for proper cellularization and mitotic cell divisions of early germ cells (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Lerit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Centrosomes ensure the faithful segregation of germ plasm into PGCs.
claims.source: Centrosomes, the microtubule (MT)-organizing centers, ensure the faithful segregation of germ plasm, a reservoir of germ cell determinants, into PGCs.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: cs and nos-Gal4 embryos had an average of ~30 pole cells at stage 5.
claims.source: Interestingly, while cs and nos-Gal4 embryos had an average of ~30 pole cells (Figure 3 A1-B3, for quantitation see panel F) casplof/ Df showed a drastic reduction in total PGC count to ~10 (Figure 3 C1-3, F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data from immunostaining.

claims.claim: casplof/Df embryos showed a drastic reduction in total PGC count to ~10 at stage 5.
claims.source: Interestingly, while cs and nos-Gal4 embryos had an average of ~30 pole cells (Figure 3 A1-B3, for quantitation see panel F) casplof/ Df showed a drastic reduction in total PGC count to ~10 (Figure 3 C1-3, F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data from immunostaining.

claims.claim: Stage 5 embryos derived from nosGal4 >UAS casp mothers displayed considerably elevated total number of PGCs.
claims.source: By contrast, stage 5 embryos derived from nosGal4 >UAS casp mothers, where casp was overexpressed (Figure 3G), displayed considerably elevated total number of PGCs (Figure 3 E1-E3, F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data from immunostaining and western blot.

claims.claim: Simultaneously overexpressing casp in the casplof/Df mothers in a germline-specific manner resulted in a significant rescue (~26 pole cells).
claims.source: To confirm that the loss of casp is specifically responsible for the reduction in the total number of PGCs, we simultaneously overexpressed casp in the casplof/Df mothers in a germline-specific manner, which resulted in a significant rescue (~26 pole cells; Figure 3 D1-D3, F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data from immunostaining showing rescue.

claims.claim: The total pole cell number in late syncytial/cellular blastoderm embryos specifically depends on casp function.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggested that the total pole cell number in late syncytial /cellular blastoderm embryos specifically depends on casp function.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from loss-of-function, gain-of-function, and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Increasing casp levels maternally is sufficient to elevate the total pole cell number substantially.
claims.source: Furthermore, increasing casp levels maternally, is sufficient to elevate the total pole cell number substantially.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the gain-of-function experiments.

claims.claim: TER94 and VAPB were the top hits in the Casp immunoprecipitation from early embryonic lysates.
claims.source: Interestingly, as in the case of brain and S2 cell lysates, TER94 and VAPB were the top hits, with germ cell determinants also identified as interactors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Discussed in a subsequent section).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents mass spectrometry data from immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: A functional protein complex between Casp, TER94, and VAPB likely exists in many different tissue/cellular contexts, including early embryos.
claims.source: These observations suggested that a functional protein complex between Casp, TER94, and VAPB likely exists in many different tissue/cellular contexts, including early embryos.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the consistent identification of these interactions across different contexts.

claims.claim: Mammalian VCP/p97 is an essential chaperone for proteostasis that modulates several ubiquitin-associated processes.
claims.source: Mammalian VCP/p97 is an essential chaperone for proteostasis that modulates several ubiquitin-associated processes (Peters et al., 1990; Dai et al., 1998; Meyer et al., 2000; Meyer, 2005; Ye, 2006; Jentsch and Rumpf, 2007; Meyer et al., 2012).

results.result: Caspar (Casp) is the Drosophila orthologue of human FAF1, originally implicated in host-defense as a negative regulator of NF-κB signaling. Both proteins share conserved domain architecture including UBA, UAS, and UBX domains with established functions in protein degradation pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C37-C49 establish the orthology relationship and functional conservation between Casp and FAF1 through sequence similarity, domain conservation, and shared roles in NF-κB regulation. The evidence is based on established knowledge, citations, and domain structure analysis (Figure 1A), providing strong support for this foundational characterization.

results.result: Maternal loss of casp leads to ~40-70% embryonic lethality independent of paternal genotype, establishing casp as a maternal effect gene. The casplof allele is a strong hypomorph retaining 5-10% protein levels. Casp mRNA is maternally deposited and ubiquitously expressed, while Casp protein is enriched in PGCs and appears to be generated post-fertilization from maternal mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C68 are well-supported by multiple complementary experiments including viability assays (Figure 1B-C), deficiency complementation tests, immunostaining (Figure 1D), western blots (Figure 1E), and expression database analysis. The genetic crosses clearly demonstrate maternal-specific effects, and the molecular characterization establishes the hypomorphic nature of the allele and expression patterns.

results.result: Maternal loss of casp results in developmental arrest before gastrulation (~40% of embryos), with conspicuous nuclear and cytoskeletal defects including irregular actin networks, disrupted nuclear spacing, and progressive deterioration of centrosome behavior. These defects are ubiquitous across the embryo and can be partially rescued by maternal casp overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C85 are strongly supported by cuticle preparations, time-lapse imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), immunostaining with multiple markers (Figure 2), and quantitative analysis of centrosome defects across nuclear cycles. The rescue experiments (C80-C81) provide genetic validation. The phenotypes are well-documented with appropriate controls and quantification.

results.result: The total number of primordial germ cells (PGCs) is directly proportional to Casp levels. Loss of casp reduces PGC count from ~30 to ~10, while overexpression increases it. This effect is specific to casp function as demonstrated by rescue experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96, C10-C11 are well-supported by quantitative immunostaining data (Figure 3) showing dose-dependent effects of Casp on PGC numbers. The loss-of-function, gain-of-function, and rescue experiments provide strong evidence for specificity. Statistical significance is demonstrated (****p<0.0001).

results.result: TER94 and VAPB are major Casp interactors in early embryos, with a functional protein complex likely existing across multiple tissue contexts. This was identified through immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry from embryonic lysates.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 and C183 are supported by proteomic data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing TER94 and VAPB as top hits in Casp immunoprecipitation experiments. The consistency across different cellular contexts (brain, S2 cells, embryos) strengthens the conclusion. However, the functional significance of these interactions in the embryonic context requires further validation.

results.result: Maternal knockdown of TER94 leads to >95% embryonic lethality with phenotypes overlapping but more severe than casp mutants, including cytoskeletal defects, centrosome abnormalities, and nuclear distribution defects. Both proteins likely perform related functions during syncytial nuclear cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C113 are supported by RNAi experiments with validated knockdown (Figure 4B), viability assays (Figure 4A), and detailed phenotypic characterization (Figure 4C-F). The comparison with casp mutants is appropriate, though the higher penetrance in TER94 knockdown could reflect differences between null (RNAi) and hypomorphic (casplof) conditions rather than distinct functions.

results.result: Maternal loss of Casp and TER94 affects pole bud formation with distinct phenotypes: casp mutants show reduced pole buds with centrosome defects, while TER94i embryos show increased but ectopically positioned pole buds that fail to survive. Both demonstrate that Casp and TER94 regulate PGC formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C128 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 5) showing pole bud defects and centrosome abnormalities. The contrasting phenotypes between casp and TER94 mutants are interesting but complicate the interpretation of their functional relationship. The claim that TER94i pole buds don't survive is based on observation but lacks direct evidence of cell death.

results.result: Oskar protein levels are directly correlated with Casp levels in the maternal germline. Loss of casp reduces Oskar levels while overexpression increases them. Oskar remains properly localized to the posterior pole in all conditions, with only levels changing. This correlates with changes in pole bud and PGC numbers across developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137, C12-C13 are well-supported by quantitative immunostaining (Figure 6A-E) showing dose-dependent effects on Oskar levels and PGC numbers. The volumetric quantification of Oskar (Figure 6D) provides rigorous measurement. The temporal analysis across nuclear cycles strengthens the conclusions. Statistical significance is demonstrated.

results.result: Casp levels influence PGC mitotic divisions as measured by phospho-histone H3 (pH3) staining. Maternal overexpression of Casp increases the proportion of pH3-positive PGCs from ~20% to ~70%, while loss of casp reduces it to <10%. This effect can be rescued by casp expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 are supported by quantitative pH3 immunostaining data (Figure 6F). The dose-dependent effects and rescue experiments provide strong evidence. However, the interpretation that this reflects changes in mitotic divisions should be tempered as pH3 marks cells in M-phase, and changes could reflect altered cell cycle timing rather than increased division frequency.

results.result: Among maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) regulators, Smaug degradation is specifically affected in casplof embryos. While Me31B and TRAL degradation patterns are unaffected, Smaug levels are modestly elevated from the start and persist in 2-3 hr casplof embryos unlike controls where Smaug is degraded.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C151 are supported by western blot time-course experiments (Figure 7) comparing multiple MZT regulators. The specificity for Smaug is demonstrated by showing unchanged patterns for Me31B, TRAL, and TER94. However, the quantification shows modest differences and the statistical significance of the persistence at 2-3 hr is not clearly stated. The biological significance of the modest elevation requires further validation.

results.result: Smaug protein levels are significantly elevated in PGCs from casplof embryos, accumulating in larger and more numerous puncta at stage 4 compared to controls. This suggests inappropriate accumulation and/or stabilization of Smaug in the absence of Casp.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 8) with quantification of both intensity and puncta number. The stage-specific analysis strengthens the conclusions. However, the interpretation of 'inappropriate accumulation and/or stabilization' (C156) is inferential and the mechanism remains unclear. The functional consequences of increased Smaug puncta are not directly tested.

results.result: Structure-function analysis reveals that the UAS and UBX domains of Casp are critical for PGC development. Deletion of UBA domain does not affect rescue or gain-of-function activity, while UBX deletion shows intermediate effects, and UAS deletion is least effective. The UAS domain is essential for supporting increased germ cell division.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C171 and C176 are supported by systematic domain deletion experiments with both rescue (Figure 9C) and gain-of-function (Figure 9D) assays. The constructs are validated by western blot (Figure 9B). The hierarchical importance of domains (UAS>UBX>UBA) is clearly demonstrated. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these domain-specific functions remain unclear.

results.result: The FFAT motif mediating Casp-VAP interaction is not essential for Casp function in PGC determination. Deletion of the FFAT motif (caspΔFFAT) rescues embryonic lethality and PGC loss, and can increase PGC numbers comparable to wild-type Casp when overexpressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C175 are supported by viability assays (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B) and PGC quantification experiments. The conclusion that Casp-VAP interaction is 'not essential or partially redundant' (C175) is reasonable given the rescue data. However, subtle functional differences might be missed, and the role of VAP in other Casp functions (e.g., somatic development) is not addressed.

results.result: Casp regulation of Oskar levels is likely zygotic rather than maternal. Evidence includes: (1) minimal Casp protein deposition in eggs with bulk protein generated post-fertilization, (2) Casp controls Smaug levels post-transcriptionally in PGCs, and (3) Smaug accumulates in germ granules where it negatively regulates Oskar translation. Loss of casp leads to excess Smaug accumulation, which likely mediates the PGC phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C195 present a mechanistic model linking Casp, Smaug, and Oskar. While individual observations are supported (Casp protein timing C190, Smaug elevation C191, Smaug's role in Oskar regulation C192-C193), the causal chain is largely inferential. The model predicts that reducing Smaug in casp mutants should rescue PGC defects, but this experiment is not performed. The 'zygotic' nature (C189) is inferred from timing but not directly tested. The model is plausible but requires additional validation.

results.result: A model is proposed where Casp functions as an adapter protein working with the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complex and TER94 to target ubiquitinated Smaug for degradation. The Casp-TER94 complex targets ubiquitinated Smaug in protein complexes. Homeostatic maintenance of Smaug levels via Casp-mediated degradation explains the reciprocal effects on Oskar and PGCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C211 present a mechanistic model based on known functions of mammalian orthologs (C206) and the observed phenotypes. While the model is internally consistent and explains the data, it lacks direct experimental validation. Key predictions are not tested: (1) Does Casp interact with SCF components? (2) Is Smaug ubiquitinated in a Casp-dependent manner? (3) Does proteasome inhibition phenocopy casp loss? The model is reasonable but speculative without these validations.

results.result: Maternal loss of either Casp or TER94 leads to partial embryonic lethality correlated with aberrant centrosome behavior, cytoskeletal abnormalities, and defective gastrulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 summarize the major phenotypic consequences and are supported by extensive data presented throughout the manuscript including viability assays, immunostaining, and time-lapse imaging. The correlation between these phenotypes is well-established.

results.result: Both Casp and TER94 proteins are ubiquitously distributed in embryos but enriched in primordial germ cells (PGCs), where they colocalize with the germ cell marker Vasa.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C62, and C117 are supported by immunostaining data (Figures 1D, 3—figure supplement 1D-E) showing both ubiquitous distribution and PGC enrichment. The colocalization with Vasa confirms PGC identity.

results.result: Oskar is the master determinant of PGC fate in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C129 state established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations. This provides important context for interpreting the Casp-Oskar relationship.

results.result: Smaug, a translational repressor and zygotic regulator of germ cell specification, is identified as a potential critical target of Casp regulation based on analysis of mid-blastula transition components.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are supported by the western blot and immunostaining data showing altered Smaug levels in casp mutants. The identification of Smaug as a target is data-driven, though the mechanistic details remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Background on insect immune system and Casp's original characterization: The insect immune system shares fundamental traits with vertebrates including humoral and innate arms. Immune components like Toll/Dorsal are pleiotropic, functioning in both immunity and development. Casp was originally identified as a negative regulator of NF-κB signaling in immune response.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C36 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. This contextualizes the novel developmental functions of Casp discovered in this study.

results.result: Background on PGC formation: In Drosophila, PGCs form at the posterior through invasion of nuclei and centrosomes into pole plasm. Centrosome behavior is crucial for PGC cellularization and mitotic divisions. Components like Gcl and Centrosomin are necessary for proper centrosome function in PGCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90, C118-C119 provide established background on PGC formation supported by citations. This contextualizes the novel findings about Casp and TER94 in PGC development.

results.result: Background on TER94: Mammalian VCP/p97 is an essential chaperone for proteostasis modulating ubiquitin-associated processes. Drosophila TER94 has been studied mainly in neurodegeneration and has roles in oogenesis and early development. TER94 is implicated in ER-associated degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 provide established background on TER94 supported by citations. This contextualizes the novel embryonic functions discovered in this study.

results.result: TER94 is a known component of pole plasm, identified through proteomic analysis of Vasa and Tudor-containing polar granule complexes along with translational machinery components.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 cite published proteomic data establishing TER94 as a pole plasm component. This provides important context for the current findings.

results.result: Summary of dual functions: Maternal loss of casp affects both PGC formation/specification via effects on Oskar accumulation, and cellular movements during gastrulation. Both somatic and germline compartments share centrosomal and cytoskeletal aberrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 accurately summarize the major findings of the study, which are well-supported by the data presented throughout.

results.result: Background and connections to MZT: Ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of Smaug, Tral, and Me31B marks MZT in Drosophila. ZGA and maternal determinant turnover occur coordinately. Many casp phenotypes are shared with mutations in ZGA components, which also affect pole plasm transmission via centrosome function.
results.evaluation: Claims C145, C196-C203 provide background on MZT and draw connections to the current findings. The parallels with ZGA mutants are noted but the mechanistic connections remain speculative.

results.result: Background on Smaug function: Smaug is a translational repressor controlling nanos and hsp83 translation through multiple mechanisms. Recent data shows Smaug accumulates in germ granules and can repress oskar translation. Smaug mutants show increased PGC numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C163 provide established and recent background on Smaug function, appropriately cited. This contextualizes the model linking Casp, Smaug, and Oskar.

results.result: Discussion context: Casp was initially characterized in immune response. Early patterning depends on maternal determinants with spatially restricted localization. Gcl controls PGC formation via centrosome function. Casp and TER94 are distinct from Gcl in having both somatic and germline functions, contributing to MZT preceding gastrulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C187 provide discussion context integrating the findings with established knowledge. The comparisons and contrasts with Gcl are appropriate and well-supported.

results.result: Connections to BMP signaling: TER94 can potentiate BMP signaling. The BMP ligand dpp is a ZGA target that influences PGC specification. PGCs require calibrated BMP signals, with excess causing PGC loss. Protein degradation machinery components regulate BMP signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C212-C217 draw connections between the current findings and BMP signaling based on published work. These connections are speculative but provide interesting context for future investigation.

results.result: Maternal loss of Casp leads to partial embryonic lethality (~40-70%), correlated with aberrant centrosome behavior, cytoskeletal abnormalities, and defective gastrulation. The phenotype is maternal-specific (independent of paternal genotype), and can be partially rescued by maternal overexpression of casp.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge these findings as solid and well-supported. Reviewer 1 states 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is solid' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the experiments are well-conducted, and the conclusions of this paper are mostly well-supported by data.' The maternal effect lethality, centrosomal defects, and cytoskeletal abnormalities are accepted as core findings.

results.result: The total number of pole buds/PGCs is directly proportional to Casp levels. Loss of Casp reduces PGC count to ~10 (from ~30 in controls), while overexpression increases PGC numbers. This effect is specific to casp function and can be rescued.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a key finding. Reviewer 1 states 'They demonstrate that PGC number...change as a result of changes in caspar expression' and notes this work 'identifies a new factor that is involved in PGC specification.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'Casp regulates PGC numbers' and 'Casp protein levels are linearly correlated to the PGC number.'

results.result: Loss of Casp results in reduction of Oskar protein levels, while gain of Casp increases Oskar levels. The change in Oskar protein levels is consistent with alteration in Casp levels, and Oskar remains properly localized to the posterior pole in all conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises significant concerns: 'Fig 6 is not quantitative, lacking even a second control staining to check for intensity variation artifacts. Therefore it shows that the distribution of Oskar protein changes in the various genotypes, but not convincingly that the level of Oskar changes as the paper claims.' This critique directly challenges the quantitative claim about Oskar levels.

results.result: TER94 and VAPB are the top hits in Casp immunoprecipitation from early embryonic lysates, suggesting a functional protein complex between Casp, TER94, and VAPB exists in multiple cellular contexts including early embryos.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern: 'The peptide counts in the mass spectrometry experiment aimed at finding protein partners for Casp are extremely low, except for Casp itself and TER94. Peptide counts of 1-2 seem to me to be of questionable significance.' This directly questions the reliability of identifying VAPB and other interactors beyond TER94.

results.result: Maternal knockdown of TER94 results in severe embryonic lethality (>95%) and phenotypes overlapping with casp mutants, including irregular nuclear distribution, perturbed F-actin localization, and centrosome defects. However, TER94 embryos show higher penetrance than casp embryos.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes: 'The pole bud phenotypes from TER94 knockdown and casp mutant shown in Fig 5 appear to be quite different. These differences are unexplained and seem inconsistent with the model proposed that the two proteins work in a common pathway. Whole embryos should also be shown, as the TER94 KD phenotype could result from a more general dysmorphism.' This raises questions about whether the phenotypes truly support a common pathway.

results.result: Maternal loss of Casp leads to loss of pole buds with defective centrosome separation, while TER94 knockdown shows increased pole bud numbers at early stages but these fail to survive, with late blastoderm embryos almost completely lacking PGCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically critiques: 'The pole bud phenotypes from TER94 knockdown and casp mutant shown in Fig 5 appear to be quite different. These differences are unexplained and seem inconsistent with the model proposed that the two proteins work in a common pathway.' The divergent phenotypes between casp and TER94 are not adequately explained.

results.result: Smaug protein levels are elevated in casplof embryos and persist longer during the maternal-to-zygotic transition (2-3 hr timepoint). Smaug accumulates in large puncta in casplof embryos and is elevated in PGCs. Casp controls Smaug levels at the post-transcriptional level.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises a critical statistical concern: 'The error bars are huge in the graphs in Fig 7H, I, and J, and in fact these changes are not statistically significant. Therefore the conclusion that "Reduction in Casp activity specifically affects Smaug degradation during the MZT" is not supported by the data in this figure.' This directly challenges the quantitative support for Smaug-specific effects.

results.result: The pattern of degradation of Me31B and TRAL proteins in casplof embryos is relatively unaffected compared to control samples.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented as supporting the specificity of the Smaug effect. While Reviewer 1 questions the statistical significance of the Smaug data, the lack of effect on Me31B and TRAL is not specifically challenged and serves as an important control.

results.result: Domain deletion analysis shows that the UAS and UBX domains are important for Casp function in PGC development. UBA domain deletion does not affect rescuing activity, UBX deletion shows intermediate activity, while UAS domain deletion is least effective for rescue.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'Based on the deletion mutant analysis, TER94 seems functionally relevant for the observed Casp phenotype.' The domain analysis is accepted as providing insight into functional requirements, though reviewers do not extensively discuss these experiments.

results.result: The FFAT motif (which mediates VAP interaction) is not essential for Casp function in PGC determination, as casp∆FFAT can rescue both lethality and PGC loss, suggesting the Casp-VAP interaction is either not essential or partially redundant.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented clearly with rescue data and is not challenged by reviewers. It provides important mechanistic insight into which protein interactions are required for Casp function in this context.

results.result: casplof is a strong hypomorphic allele and not a null, as trace amounts of Casp protein (5-10% of wild-type) are present in embryos from casplof/casplof and casplof/Df mothers.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 directly challenges the nomenclature: 'A PiggyBac insertion allele casp[c04227] is used throughout the paper and referred to as a loss-of-function allele (casp[lof]). While the authors avoid the terms "null" or "amorph" and on one occasion refer to the allele as a "strong hypomorph", nevertheless terming it a "loss-of-function" allele is misleading. This is because the phenotype of the allele when homozygous is different from the phenotype produced when heterozygous over a deficiency.'

results.result: The authors propose that PGC-specific phenotypes upon loss of casp are mediated by excess accumulation of Smaug, and that Casp functions as an adapter protein working with the SCF complex and TER94 to target ubiquitinated Smaug for degradation, thereby maintaining homeostatic Smaug levels.
results.evaluation: This is a proposed model rather than directly demonstrated mechanism. Reviewer 1's concerns about the statistical significance of Smaug data undermine this model. Reviewer 2 notes 'the functional relationships among molecules shown here (Casp, TER94, Osk) and other genes previously known to regulate these processes remain unclear,' indicating the mechanistic model needs further validation.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the maternal effect lethality and basic characterization of casp mutants (C52-C55, C3-C7). OpenEval finds the evidence well-supported by multiple complementary experiments. Peer reviewers also accept these as solid core findings, though Reviewer 1 challenges the 'loss-of-function' nomenclature for the allele (C65), which OpenEval does not flag as problematic.

Both address centrosomal defects and cytoskeletal abnormalities (C71-C83). OpenEval finds these strongly supported by cuticle preparations, time-lapse imaging, and immunostaining with quantification. Peer reviewers agree these findings are solid and well-supported by data.

Both evaluate the effect of Casp on PGC numbers (C91-C96, C10-C11). OpenEval finds strong support from quantitative immunostaining showing dose-dependent effects with statistical significance. Peer reviewers accept this as a key finding, with Reviewer 1 noting this identifies a new factor in PGC specification and Reviewer 2 confirming the linear correlation between Casp levels and PGC number.

Both address PGC-related phenotypes. OpenEval R8 focuses on Oskar levels and PGC numbers (C130-C137, C12-C13), while Peer R2 includes some overlapping claims about PGC regulation (C134-C137, C139-C141). OpenEval finds the volumetric quantification rigorous, but peer reviewers raise concerns about quantification methodology.

Both evaluate claims about Oskar regulation (C12-C13, C130-C133). OpenEval finds the volumetric quantification of Oskar provides rigorous measurement with statistical significance. However, Reviewer 1 directly challenges this: 'Fig 6 is not quantitative, lacking even a second control staining...not convincingly that the level of Oskar changes as the paper claims.' This represents a significant disagreement on data quality.

Both address mitotic effects (C139-C141). OpenEval finds support from pH3 immunostaining but notes the interpretation should be tempered as changes could reflect altered cell cycle timing. Peer reviewers accept the PGC-related findings broadly but do not specifically discuss the pH3/mitotic division interpretation.

Both evaluate the proteomic identification of TER94 and VAPB as Casp interactors (C97-C98, C183). OpenEval finds support from consistency across contexts but notes functional significance requires validation. Reviewer 1 expresses significant concern: 'Peptide counts of 1-2 seem to me to be of questionable significance,' directly questioning the reliability of identifying VAPB and other interactors beyond TER94.

Both evaluate TER94 knockdown phenotypes (C105-C113). OpenEval finds support from RNAi experiments with validated knockdown, noting higher penetrance could reflect null vs hypomorphic differences. Reviewer 1 raises concerns that the pole bud phenotypes from TER94 knockdown and casp mutant 'appear to be quite different' and 'seem inconsistent with the model proposed that the two proteins work in a common pathway.'

Both address pole bud defects and centrosome abnormalities (C120-C126). OpenEval notes the contrasting phenotypes between casp and TER94 mutants complicate interpretation of their functional relationship. Reviewer 1 specifically critiques that these phenotypic differences are 'unexplained and seem inconsistent with the model,' representing agreement that this is problematic for the proposed common pathway model.

Both evaluate Smaug degradation during MZT (C146-C151). OpenEval finds support from western blot time-course but notes modest differences and unclear statistical significance. Reviewer 1 directly challenges: 'The error bars are huge...these changes are not statistically significant. Therefore the conclusion that "Reduction in Casp activity specifically affects Smaug degradation during the MZT" is not supported.' This is a major disagreement on statistical rigor.

Both address Smaug accumulation in embryos (C152-C156). OpenEval finds support from immunostaining with quantification but notes the interpretation is inferential. Reviewer 1's concerns about statistical significance of the western blot data (overlapping with R10/R7 comparison) also undermine confidence in the Smaug accumulation claims, as they are part of the same mechanistic story.

Both address the specificity of effects on Smaug vs other MZT regulators (C147). OpenEval notes Me31B and TRAL are unchanged, supporting specificity. Peer reviewers do not specifically challenge the lack of effect on these controls, and this serves as an important control even though the Smaug quantification itself is disputed.

Both evaluate domain deletion experiments (C164-C171, C176). OpenEval finds strong support from systematic rescue and gain-of-function assays showing hierarchical domain importance. Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'Based on the deletion mutant analysis, TER94 seems functionally relevant for the observed Casp phenotype,' accepting these findings.

Both evaluate the role of Casp-VAP interaction (C172-C175). OpenEval finds support from rescue data for the conclusion that this interaction is 'not essential or partially redundant.' Peer reviewers do not challenge this finding, accepting the rescue data as presented.

Both address the mechanistic model linking Casp, Smaug, and Oskar (C188-C195, C194). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN, noting the causal chain is inferential and key predictions untested. Reviewer 1's concerns about Smaug data statistical significance undermine the model. Reviewer 2 notes 'the functional relationships among molecules...remain unclear,' indicating the mechanistic model needs validation. Both agree the model is inadequately supported.

Both evaluate the proposed ubiquitin-proteasome mechanism (C204-C211, C207-C211). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of direct experimental validation for key predictions. This overlaps with peer concerns about the mechanistic model being inadequately validated, as both address the proposed molecular mechanism underlying the phenotypes.

Both address the major phenotypic consequences (C3-C7). OpenEval finds these well-supported by extensive data throughout the manuscript. Peer reviewers accept these as solid core findings, with all reviewers acknowledging the evidence is strong for the basic phenotypic characterization.

OpenEval R2 includes C65 (hypomorphic allele characterization) and finds it supported. Peer R11 specifically challenges the 'loss-of-function' nomenclature as misleading, noting the allele behaves differently when homozygous vs heterozygous over deficiency. This represents a disagreement on appropriate genetic terminology and interpretation.
